notes.front: What is section 1231 property?
notes.back: Real or depreciable property used in a trade or business and held for more than 1 year, among other listed items.
notes.explanation: Its sale or exchange is a section 1231 transaction, reported in Part I of Form 4797.
notes.example: Like a delivery van a bakery has used for three years and then sells.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 4797 (2025), “Part I: Section 1231 transactions”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Sales or exchanges of real or depreciable property used in a trade or business and held for more than 1 year.

notes.front: What is the Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System (MACRS)?
notes.back: The system used to recover the basis of most business and investment property placed in service after 1986, through depreciation.
notes.explanation: It contains a general and an alternative depreciation system, with different methods and recovery periods.
notes.example: Like a fixed timetable that spreads a machine’s cost over the years it earns income.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Figuring Depreciation Under MACRS”, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: The Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System (MACRS) is used to recover the basis of most business and investment property placed in service after 1986. MACRS consists of two depreciation systems, the General Depreciation System (GDS) and the Alternative Depreciation System (ADS).

notes.front: What is the half-year convention?
notes.back: A rule treating all property placed in service or disposed of during the year as placed in service or disposed of at mid-year.
notes.explanation: For a 12-month year this allows half a year of depreciation in the first and last years.
notes.example: Like a hotel charging half a night for any check-in, whatever the hour.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “The half-year convention”, PDF p. 34
notes.evidence: Under this convention, you treat all property placed in service or disposed of during a tax year as placed in service or disposed of at the midpoint of the year.

notes.front: What is the mid-quarter convention?
notes.back: A rule treating property placed in service or disposed of during a quarter as placed in service or disposed of at that quarter’s midpoint.
notes.explanation: It allows 1½ months of depreciation for that quarter in a 12-month year.
notes.example: Like billing a gym membership from the middle of the quarter you joined in.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “The mid-quarter convention”, PDF p. 34
notes.evidence: Under this convention, you treat all property placed in service or disposed of during any quarter of the tax year as placed in service or disposed of at the midpoint of that quarter.

notes.front: What is the mid-month convention?
notes.back: A rule treating property placed in service or disposed of during a month as placed in service or disposed of at that month’s midpoint.
notes.explanation: It applies to nonresidential real property, residential rental property and railroad grading or tunnel bores.
notes.example: Like counting a tenant who moves in on any day in March as arriving on 15 March.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “The mid-month convention”, PDF p. 34
notes.evidence: Use this convention for nonresidential real property, residential rental property, and any railroad grading or tunnel bore. Under this convention, you treat all property placed in service or disposed of during a month as placed in service or disposed of at the midpoint of the month.

notes.front: What is the section 179 deduction?
notes.back: An election to deduct all or part of the cost of qualifying property, up to a limit, in the year it is placed in service.
notes.explanation: It is taken instead of recovering that cost through depreciation; estates and trusts cannot elect it.
notes.example: Like writing off a new printer’s whole cost at once instead of over several years.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Electing the Section 179 Deduction”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: You can elect to recover all or part of the cost of certain qualifying property, up to a limit, by deducting it in the year you place the property in service. This is the section 179 deduction.

notes.front: What is the special depreciation allowance?
notes.back: An extra first-year deduction for certain property, taken after any section 179 deduction and before regular MACRS depreciation.
notes.explanation: It applies only for the year the property is placed in service; it is often called bonus depreciation.
notes.example: Like a bonus instalment paid up front before the regular instalments begin.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Claiming the Special Depreciation Allowance”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: The allowance applies only for the first year you place the property in service. The allowance is an additional deduction you can take after any section 179 deduction and before you figure regular depreciation under MACRS for the year you place the property in service.

notes.front: What is listed property?
notes.back: Property such as passenger automobiles, business aircraft, other transport property and property generally used for entertainment or recreation.
notes.explanation: Such property faces extra rules: a business-use test, recordkeeping and passenger automobile limits.
notes.example: Like a company car or a video camera: assets easily put to personal use.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “What Is Listed Property?”, PDF p. 52
notes.evidence: Listed property is any of the following. • Passenger automobiles (as defined later). • Business aircraft (discussed later). • Any other property used for transportation, unless it is an excepted vehicle. • Property generally used for entertainment, recreation, or amusement

notes.front: What are section 197 intangibles?
notes.back: Certain acquired intangibles, such as goodwill, going concern value and a covenant not to compete, that must be amortised over 15 years.
notes.explanation: Amortisation starts with the later of the month acquired or the month the business begins.
notes.example: Like the goodwill paid for when buying a well-known local shop.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 4562 (2025), “Certain section 197 intangibles”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: The following intangibles must be amortized over 15 years (180 months) starting with the later of (a) the month the intangibles were acquired, or (b) the month the trade or business or activity engaged in for the production of income begins. • Goodwill. • Going concern value.

notes.front: What is the de minimis safe harbor for tangible property?
notes.back: An election to deduct small amounts paid for tangible property that would otherwise be capitalised, if they are also expensed in the books.
notes.explanation: Without it, costs to acquire buildings, equipment or furniture must generally be capitalised.
notes.example: Like expensing a $300 office chair instead of depreciating it over seven years.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “De Minimis Safe Harbor for Tangible Property”, PDF p. 42
notes.evidence: if you elect to use the de minimis safe harbor for tangible property, you may deduct de minimis amounts paid to acquire or produce certain tangible property if these amounts are deducted by you for financial accounting purposes or in keeping your books and records.

notes.front: What is the basis of property bought for use in a business?
notes.explanation: Property you construct or produce instead has its costs capitalised as basis, subject to the uniform capitalization rules.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Business Assets”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: If you purchase property to use in your business, your basis is usually its actual cost to you. If you construct, create, or otherwise produce property, you must capitalize the costs as your basis.

notes.front: A workshop builds its own storage shed, spending $6,000 on materials and $3,000 on hired labour. Its crew’s time building the shed would otherwise have gone to billable work worth $2,000. What is the shed’s basis?
notes.choicesExplained: B adds lost profit, which is not a cost paid. C leaves out labour costs actually paid.
notes.explanation: Costs of producing the property are capitalised: $6,000 + $3,000 = $9,000.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Business Assets”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: If you construct, create, or otherwise produce property, you must capitalize the costs as your basis.

notes.front: Which improvements increase the basis of property?
notes.back: Items properly added to a capital account, including improvements with a useful life of more than 1 year.
notes.explanation: Replacing an entire roof is one of Pub. 551’s examples of an increase.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Increases to Basis”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Increase the basis of any property by all items properly added to a capital account. These include the cost of any improvements having a useful life of more than 1 year.

notes.front: What are two deductions that reduce the basis of business property?
notes.explanation: Casualty loss deductions and insurance reimbursements also reduce basis.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Table 1. Examples of Increases and Decreases to Basis”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: Casualty or theft loss deductions and insurance reimbursements Certain vehicle credits Section 179 deduction Depreciation

notes.front: A machine cost $50,000. The owner added a $10,000 upgrade with a 5-year useful life and has claimed $22,000 of depreciation. What is its adjusted basis?
notes.choicesExplained: B leaves out the capital improvement. C ignores the depreciation.
notes.explanation: Improvements over 1 year add to basis; depreciation reduces it: $50,000 + $10,000 − $22,000 = $38,000.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Increases to Basis”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: These include the cost of any improvements having a useful life of more than 1 year.

notes.front: What is the basis for depreciation of property changed from personal to business use?
notes.back: The lesser of its fair market value or its adjusted basis on the date of the change.
notes.explanation: Renting out a former main home is Pub. 551’s example of such a change.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Property Changed From Personal Use”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: The basis for depreciation is the lesser of the following amounts. • The FMV of the property on the date of the change, or • Your adjusted basis on the date of the change.

notes.front: Nina starts using her personal car, bought for $30,000, wholly in her new business. On that date it is worth $18,000. What is its basis for depreciation?
notes.choicesExplained: A uses cost, though the value is lower. C averages the two, which no rule does.
notes.explanation: The lesser of $18,000 fair market value and $30,000 adjusted basis is $18,000.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Property Changed From Personal Use”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: The basis for depreciation is the lesser of the following amounts. • The FMV of the property on the date of the change, or • Your adjusted basis on the date of the change.

notes.front: Which form reports the sale of real property or depreciable property used in a trade or business?
notes.explanation: The same form reports involuntary conversions (other than casualty or theft) of business property.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 4797 (2025), “Purpose of Form”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Use Form 4797 to report the following. • The sale or exchange of: 1. Real property used in your trade or business; 2. Depreciable and amortizable tangible property used in your trade or business

notes.front: Which sale belongs on Form 4797?
notes.choices:
A) A shop owner sells a display cabinet used in the business for 4 years
B) A retailer sells stock from its shelves
C) An individual sells shares held as an investment
notes.choicesExplained: B is inventory, reported through gross receipts. C is a capital asset sale reported on Form 8949 and Schedule D.
notes.explanation: The cabinet is depreciable property used in the trade or business.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 4797 (2025), “Purpose of Form”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Depreciable and amortizable tangible property used in your trade or business

notes.front: Is inventory held for sale to customers section 1231 property?
notes.back: No. Sales of inventory are not section 1231 transactions.
notes.explanation: Self-created copyrights and similar property are also excluded.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 4797 (2025), “Transactions to which section 1231 does not apply”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Section 1231 transactions do not include sales or exchanges of: 6 • Inventory or property held primarily for sale to customers

notes.front: How is a net section 1231 loss treated, and how is a net section 1231 gain treated?
notes.back: A net loss is ordinary. A net gain is ordinary up to nonrecaptured section 1231 losses; the rest is long-term capital gain.
notes.explanation: All section 1231 gains and losses for the year are combined first.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Section 1231 Gains and Losses: Treatment as ordinary or capital”, PDF p. 41
notes.evidence: If you have a net section 1231 loss, it is ordinary loss. • If you have a net section 1231 gain, it is ordinary in- come up to the amount of your nonrecaptured section 1231 losses from previous years. The rest, if any, is long-term capital gain.

notes.front: Nonrecaptured section 1231 losses are net section 1231 losses from the previous {{c1::5}} years not yet applied against a net section 1231 gain.
notes.explanation: They are applied starting with the earliest loss.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Nonrecaptured section 1231 losses”, PDF p. 41
notes.evidence: Your nonrecaptured section 1231 losses are your net section 1231 losses for the previous 5 years that have not been applied against a net section 1231 gain.

notes.front: A sole proprietor had a net section 1231 loss of $3,000 in 2022 and no other section 1231 activity until 2025, when she has a net section 1231 gain of $10,000. How is the 2025 gain treated?
notes.choices:
A) $10,000 long-term capital gain
B) $10,000 ordinary income
C) $3,000 ordinary income and $7,000 long-term capital gain
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the 5-year lookback. C treats all the gain as ordinary.
notes.explanation: The 2022 loss is within 5 years: $10,000 − $3,000 recaptured as ordinary = $7,000 long-term capital gain.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Nonrecaptured section 1231 losses”, PDF p. 41
notes.evidence: if in any of your 5 preceding tax years you had section 1231 losses, a net gain for the current year from the sale of section 1231 assets is ordinary gain to the extent of your prior losses.

notes.front: What property qualifies for like-kind exchange treatment?
notes.back: Only real property held for investment or for productive use in a trade or business, not held primarily for sale.
notes.explanation: Both the property given up and the property received must be held that way.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Qualifying Property”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: The nonrecognition rules for like-kind exchanges apply only to exchanges of real property, as defined in Regulations section 1.1031(a)-1(a)(3), held for investment or for productive use in your trade or business and not held primarily for sale.

notes.front: Which trade can be a like-kind exchange with no gain recognised?
notes.back: C: rental land for an office building.
notes.choices:
A) A contractor trades an old excavator for a new one
B) A developer trades lots it holds for sale for other lots
C) An investor trades rental land for an office building to rent out
notes.choicesExplained: A involves equipment, which is not real property. C involves property held primarily for sale.
notes.explanation: Both sides are real property held for investment or business use.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Qualifying Property”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: Buildings, land, and rental property are examples of property that may qualify.

notes.front: Under MACRS, automobiles, taxis, buses and trucks are {{c1::5}}-year property.
notes.explanation: Office furniture and fixtures, by contrast, are 7-year property.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Which Property Class Applies Under GDS?”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: 5-year property. a. Automobiles, taxis, buses, helicopters, and trucks.

notes.front: A law firm buys desks, filing cabinets and a safe. What MACRS property class are they?
notes.choices:
A) 5-year property
B) 7-year property
C) 39-year property
notes.choicesExplained: A is for cars, trucks and office machinery. C is for nonresidential real property.
notes.explanation: Office furniture and fixtures such as desks, files and safes are 7-year property.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Which Property Class Applies Under GDS?”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: Office furniture and fixtures (such as desks, files, and safes).

notes.front: Over what recovery period is residential rental property depreciated under the general depreciation system?
notes.explanation: Residential rental property uses the mid-month convention.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Office in the home”, PDF p. 33
notes.evidence: depreciate the part used as an office as residential rental property over 27.5 years.

notes.front: Over what recovery period is nonresidential real property depreciated under the general depreciation system?
notes.back: 39 years (31.5 years if placed in service before 13 May 1993).
notes.explanation: A home office in a single-family residence is depreciated this way.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Office in the home”, PDF p. 33
notes.evidence: depreciate that part of your home as nonresidential real property over 39 years (31.5 years if you began using it for business before May 13, 1993).

notes.front: An investor buys a small shop building and, separately, a duplex to let to tenants. What recovery periods apply?
notes.choices:
A) Shop 27.5 years; duplex 39 years
B) Both 27.5 years
C) Shop 39 years; duplex 27.5 years
notes.choicesExplained: B treats commercial property as residential. C reverses them.
notes.explanation: A shop is nonresidential real property (39 years); a let duplex is residential rental property (27.5 years).
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Office in the home”, PDF p. 33
notes.evidence: depreciate that part of your home as nonresidential real property over 39 years

notes.front: The half-year convention applies when {{c1::neither the mid-quarter nor the mid-month convention}} applies.
notes.explanation: The mid-month convention covers real property; the mid-quarter one applies when too much is placed in service in the last quarter.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “The half-year convention”, PDF p. 34
notes.evidence: Use this convention if neither the mid-quarter convention nor the mid-month convention applies.

notes.front: When must the mid-quarter convention be used?
notes.back: When more than 40% of the depreciable bases of MACRS property placed in service in the year falls in its last 3 months.
notes.explanation: Real property and property placed in service and disposed of in the same year are left out of the test.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “The mid-quarter convention”, PDF p. 34
notes.evidence: the total depreciable bases of MACRS property you placed in service during the last 3 months of the tax year

notes.front: A calendar-year business places in service $30,000 of equipment in March and $25,000 in November 2025, and no real property. Which convention applies?
notes.choices:
A) Half-year
B) Mid-month
C) Mid-quarter
notes.choicesExplained: A would apply only if the last quarter held 40% or less. C is for real property.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “The mid-quarter convention”, PDF p. 34
notes.evidence: are more than 40% of the total depreciable bases of all MACRS property you placed in service during the entire year.

notes.front: A calendar-year business places in service $40,000 of equipment in April and $10,000 in December 2025. Which convention applies to the equipment?
notes.choices:
A) Half-year
B) Mid-quarter
C) Mid-month
notes.choicesExplained: B needs more than 40% in the last quarter. C is for real property.
notes.explanation: $10,000 ÷ $50,000 = 20%, not more than 40%, so the half-year convention applies.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “The half-year convention”, PDF p. 34
notes.evidence: Use this convention if neither the mid-quarter convention nor the mid-month convention applies.

notes.front: A calendar-year landlord places a residential rental building in service on 3 September 2025. How many months of depreciation does the mid-month convention allow for 2025?
notes.choicesExplained: A counts all of September. C applies a half-year.
notes.explanation: Half of September + October, November, December = 0.5 + 3 = 3.5 months.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “The mid-month convention”, PDF p. 34
notes.evidence: This means that a one-half month of depreciation is allowed for the month the property is placed in service or disposed of.

notes.front: What are the 2025 section 179 dollar limit and phase-out threshold?
notes.back: $2,500,000, reduced by the amount by which qualifying property placed in service exceeds $4,000,000.
notes.explanation: These limits apply to each taxpayer, not to each business.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “What’s New for 2025: Section 179 deduction dollar limits”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: For tax years beginning in 2025, the maximum section 179 expense deduction is $2,500,000. This limit is reduced by the amount by which the cost of section 179 property placed in service during the tax year exceeds $4,000,000.

notes.front: In 2025 a manufacturer places in service $4,300,000 of section 179 property. What is its maximum section 179 deduction before the business income limit?
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the phase-out. C is the excess itself, not the reduced limit.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “What’s New for 2025: Section 179 deduction dollar limits”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: This limit is reduced by the amount by which the cost of section 179 property placed in service during the tax year exceeds $4,000,000.

notes.front: After the dollar limit, what second limit applies to the section 179 deduction?
notes.back: The business income limit: taxable income from trades or businesses actively conducted during the year.
notes.explanation: The dollar limit gives a tentative deduction; the business income limit then sets the actual one.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Dollar Limits”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: After you apply the dollar limit to determine a tentative deduction, you must apply the business income limit (described later) to determine your actual section 179 deduction.

notes.front: A sole proprietor buys a $60,000 machine in 2025 and elects section 179 for all of it. His taxable income from active businesses, before the deduction, is $45,000. What can he deduct under section 179 in 2025?
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the business income limit. C ignores the deduction altogether.
notes.explanation: The deduction is limited to $45,000 of business income; the other $15,000 is not deductible this year.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Dollar Limits”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: you must apply the business income limit (described later) to determine your actual section 179 deduction.

notes.front: Which of these can elect the section 179 deduction for equipment used in its business?
notes.choices:
A) A sole proprietorship
B) A trust carrying on a farm
C) An estate running the decedent’s shop
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are a trust and an estate, which cannot elect it.
notes.explanation: Estates and trusts are barred from the section 179 deduction.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Electing the Section 179 Deduction”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: Estates and trusts cannot elect the section 179 deduction.

notes.front: What is the maximum 2025 section 179 deduction for a sport utility vehicle?
notes.explanation: This cap for sport utility vehicles is far below the general $2,500,000 limit.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “What’s New for 2025”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: the maximum section 179 expense deduction for sport utility vehicles placed in service in tax years beginning in 2025 is $31,300.

notes.front: What special depreciation allowance applies to certain qualified property acquired and placed in service after 19 January 2025?
notes.explanation: The taxpayer can elect 40% instead for the first tax year ending after 19 January 2025.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “What’s New for 2025”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: reinstated the 100% special depreciation allowance for certain qualified property acquired and placed in service after January 19, 2025

notes.front: What special depreciation allowance applies to certain qualified property acquired before 20 January 2025 and placed in service in 2025?
notes.explanation: Pub. 946 describes this as a phase-down of the special depreciation allowance.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “What’s New for 2025”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: The special depreciation allowance is limited to 40% for certain qualified property acquired after September 27, 2017, and placed in service after December 31, 2024, and before January 1, 2026

notes.front: A business signs a binding contract and acquires a $200,000 machine on 10 January 2025 and places it in service in March 2025. A second machine, also $200,000, is acquired on 1 March 2025 and placed in service in April 2025. What is the total special depreciation allowance, with no elections?
notes.choicesExplained: A gives 100% to both. C gives 40% to both.
notes.explanation: First machine (acquired before 20 January): 40% × $200,000 = $80,000. Second: 100% × $200,000 = $200,000. Total $280,000.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “What’s New for 2025”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: reinstated the 100% special depreciation allowance for certain qualified property acquired and placed in service after January 19, 2025

notes.front: In the year property is placed in service, the special depreciation allowance is taken after any section 179 deduction and {{c1::before regular MACRS depreciation}}.
notes.explanation: Each step reduces the basis left for the next.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Claiming the Special Depreciation Allowance”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: The allowance is an additional deduction you can take after any section 179 deduction and before you figure regular depreciation under MACRS

notes.front: A $100,000 machine qualifying for the 40% allowance is placed in service in 2025. The owner elects $30,000 of section 179. What is the special depreciation allowance?
notes.choicesExplained: A applies 40% before the section 179 deduction. C applies 40% to the section 179 amount.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Claiming the Special Depreciation Allowance”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: The allowance is an additional deduction you can take after any section 179 deduction and before you figure regular depreciation under MACRS

notes.front: What business-use test must listed property meet for section 179, the special allowance and accelerated MACRS?
notes.back: It must be used more than 50% of its total use for qualified business use.
notes.explanation: Investment use cannot be counted as qualified business use for this test.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “What Is the Business-Use Requirement?”, PDF p. 54
notes.evidence: To meet this requirement, listed property must be used predominantly (more than 50% of its total use) for qualified

notes.front: A consultant’s car is driven 9,000 miles in 2025: 4,000 for business, 1,000 to manage her investments and 4,000 for personal trips. Does it meet the listed property business-use test?
notes.choices:
A) Yes: 5,000 of 9,000 miles is over 50%
B) Yes: personal use is under 50%
C) No: qualified business use is 4,000 ÷ 9,000, about 44%
notes.choicesExplained: A counts investment miles, which don’t count for this test. C tests the wrong figure.
notes.explanation: Only business miles count: 4,000 ÷ 9,000 ≈ 44%, not more than 50%.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Overview of Depreciation”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: do not treat investment use as qualified business use when determining whether the business-use requirement for listed property is met.

notes.front: What may happen if listed property stops meeting the business-use test in a later year?
notes.back: Excess depreciation claimed in earlier years may have to be recaptured into income.
notes.explanation: Depreciation is then figured by the straight line method over the alternative depreciation system’s recovery period.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Additional Rules for Listed Property”, PDF p. 52
notes.evidence: method over the ADS recovery period. You may also have to recapture (include in income) any excess depreciation claimed in previous years.

notes.front: What are the first-year depreciation limits for a passenger automobile placed in service in 2025, with and without the special allowance?
notes.explanation: Later years are the same either way: $19,600, then $11,800, then $7,060 a year.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Depreciation limits on cars, trucks, and vans”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: for which the Code section 168(k) additional first-year depreciation deduction applies are first tax year, $20,200; second tax year, $19,600; third tax year, $11,800; and each succeeding year, $7,060.

notes.front: A sole proprietor buys a $60,000 passenger car in 2025, uses it 100% for business and claims the special allowance. What is the most depreciation (including section 179 and the allowance) she can deduct for 2025?
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the passenger automobile limit. C is the limit when the special allowance does not apply.
notes.explanation: The first-year limit with the special allowance is $20,200, and the $60,000 cost is far above it.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Depreciation limits on cars, trucks, and vans”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: for which the Code section 168(k) additional first-year depreciation deduction applies are first tax year, $20,200; second tax year, $19,600; third tax year, $11,800; and each succeeding year, $7,060.

notes.front: On a sale of section 1245 property, how much of the gain is ordinary income?
notes.back: The lesser of the depreciation and amortisation allowed or allowable, or the gain realised.
notes.explanation: Any remaining gain is section 1231 gain.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Section 1245 Property: Gain Treated as Ordinary Income”, PDF p. 43
notes.evidence: The gain treated as ordinary income on the sale, exchange, or involuntary conversion of section 1245 property, including a sale and leaseback transaction, is the lesser of the following amounts. 1. The depreciation and amortization allowed or allowable on the property. 2. The gain realized on the disposition

notes.front: Equipment bought for $50,000 has had $35,000 of depreciation, leaving adjusted basis of $15,000. It is sold for $58,000. How is the $43,000 gain split?
notes.choices:
A) $43,000 section 1231
B) $43,000 ordinary
C) $35,000 ordinary; $8,000 section 1231
notes.choicesExplained: B makes gain above the depreciation ordinary. C ignores recapture.
notes.explanation: Gain $58,000 − $15,000 = $43,000. Ordinary = lesser of $35,000 depreciation or $43,000 gain = $35,000; rest $8,000 is section 1231 gain.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Section 1245 Property: Gain Treated as Ordinary Income”, PDF p. 43
notes.evidence: The depreciation and amortization allowed or allowable on the property. 2. The gain realized on the disposition (the amount realized from the disposition minus the adjusted basis of the property).

notes.front: The same kind of equipment, adjusted basis $15,000 after $35,000 of depreciation, is instead sold for $20,000. How much is ordinary income?
notes.choicesExplained: A exceeds the gain realised. C ignores recapture.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Section 1245 Property: Gain Treated as Ordinary Income”, PDF p. 43
notes.evidence: is the lesser of the following amounts. 1. The depreciation and amortization allowed or allowable on the property. 2. The gain realized on the disposition

notes.front: To what extent is gain on section 1250 property treated as ordinary income?
notes.back: To the extent of additional depreciation: depreciation beyond what the straight-line method would give, for property held over 1 year.
notes.explanation: If section 1250 property becomes section 1245 property through a change of use, it can never again be treated as section 1250 property.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Section 1250 Property”, PDF p. 44
notes.evidence: Gain on the disposition of section 1250 property is treated as ordinary income to the extent of additional depreciation allowed or allowable on the property.

notes.front: On disposing of a section 197 intangible, how much of any gain is ordinary income?
notes.back: Gain up to the allowable amortisation is recaptured as ordinary income.
notes.explanation: A section 197 intangible is treated as depreciable property used in the trade or business.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 4562 (2025), “Certain section 197 intangibles”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: A section 197 intangible is treated as depreciable property used in your trade or business. When you dispose of a section 197 intangible, any gain on the disposition, up to the amount of allowable amortization, is recaptured as ordinary income.

notes.front: On 1 July 2025 a buyer pays $180,000 for goodwill as part of buying a going business and starts running it that month. What is the 2025 amortisation deduction for the goodwill?
notes.choicesExplained: A takes a full year. C expenses the whole cost.
notes.explanation: $180,000 ÷ 180 months = $1,000 a month; July–December = 6 months = $6,000.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 4562 (2025), “Certain section 197 intangibles”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: The following intangibles must be amortized over 15 years (180 months) starting with the later of (a) the month the intangibles were acquired

notes.front: Which cost is a section 197 intangible amortised over 15 years?
notes.back: C: the covenant not to compete.
notes.choices:
A) The inventory bought with the business
B) A delivery truck bought with the business
C) A covenant not to compete signed when buying a business
notes.choicesExplained: B is 5-year MACRS property. C is inventory, recovered through cost of goods sold.
notes.explanation: A covenant not to compete entered into in connection with acquiring a business is on the list.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 4562 (2025), “Certain section 197 intangibles”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: A covenant not to compete entered into in connection with the acquisition of a business.

notes.front: When can an incorrect depreciation deduction be corrected on an amended return?
notes.back: Among other cases, when the incorrect amount came from a mathematical error made in any year.
notes.explanation: Where an amended return is not allowed, changing the accounting method may be the way to claim the correct amount.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Filing an Amended Return”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: You claimed the incorrect amount because of a mathematical error made in any year.

notes.front: Which form is generally filed to change a method of accounting for depreciation?
notes.explanation: Changing the method generally needs approval.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Changing Your Accounting Method”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: You must generally file Form 3115 to request a change in your method of accounting for depreciation.

notes.front: For three years in a row a landlord has depreciated a rental house over 39 years instead of 27.5 years. How is this generally corrected?
notes.choices:
A) Amend only the most recent return
B) Nothing can be done
C) File Form 3115 to change the method of accounting
notes.choicesExplained: A: using the same impermissible method on two or more returns adopts a method, so an amended return is generally not the fix. C is wrong.
notes.explanation: Using the same impermissible method in two or more consecutive returns adopts it as a method of accounting.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Adoption of accounting method defined”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: by using the same impermissible method of determining depreciation in two or more consecut

notes.front: Without an applicable financial statement, up to what amount per item or invoice can be deducted under the de minimis safe harbor?
notes.explanation: A taxpayer with an applicable financial statement can use $5,000.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “De Minimis Safe Harbor for Tangible Property”, PDF p. 42
notes.evidence: minimis safe harbor to deduct amounts paid for tangible property up to $2,500 per item or invoice.

notes.front: A sole proprietor with no applicable financial statement elects the de minimis safe harbor. She buys a $1,800 laptop and a $3,200 printer, each on its own invoice, and expenses both in her books. Which can she deduct under the safe harbor?
notes.choices:
A) Both
B) Neither
C) The laptop only
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the $2,500 cap. C ignores the safe harbor.
notes.explanation: $1,800 is within $2,500 per invoice; $3,200 is not, so the printer is capitalised.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “De Minimis Safe Harbor for Tangible Property”, PDF p. 42
notes.evidence: minimis safe harbor to deduct amounts paid for tangible property up to $2,500 per item or invoice.

notes.front: When is an expense on property an improvement that must be capitalised?
notes.back: When it results in a betterment, restores the property, or adapts it to a new or different use.
notes.explanation: Repairs and maintenance may be deducted if capitalisation is not required.
notes.source: Publication 527 (2025), Residential Rental Property, “Repairs and Improvements”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: You must capitalize any expense you pay to improve your rental property. An expense is for an improvement if it results in a betterment to your property, restores your property, or adapts your property to a new or different use.

notes.front: Which cost to a rental house is an improvement rather than a repair?
notes.choices:
A) Adding a new bedroom extension
B) Fixing a leaking tap
C) Repainting a scuffed hallway
notes.choicesExplained: B and C maintain the property without bettering, restoring or adapting it.
notes.explanation: Enlarging or expanding the property is a betterment.
notes.source: Publication 527 (2025), Residential Rental Property, “Betterments”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: Expenses that may result in a betterment to your property include expenses for fixing a pre-existing defect or condition, enlarging or expanding your property, or increasing the capacity, strength, or quality of your property.

notes.front: What may still let a taxpayer deduct a cost that counts as an improvement to a building or equipment?
notes.explanation: Costs of repairs and improvements should be recorded separately.
notes.source: Publication 527 (2025), Residential Rental Property, “Safe harbor for routine maintenance”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: If you determine that your cost was for an improvement to a building or equipment, you may still be able to deduct your cost under the routine maintenance safe harbor.

notes.front: How does the section 179 deduction differ from the special depreciation allowance in who can use it and what caps it?
notes.back: Section 179 is an election with dollar and business income limits, barred to estates and trusts; the allowance is a first-year percentage taken afterwards.
notes.explanation: When both apply, section 179 comes first and the allowance applies to the basis left.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Claiming the Special Depreciation Allowance”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: The allowance is an additional deduction you can take after any section 179 deduction
